outcomes.text: Explain that each auxiliary heads its own VP and takes a VP complement, and name the four auxiliary types (MOD, PERF, PROG, PASS).
Apply the rule that only the first verb of a sequence carries the tense feature.
Distinguish negation by not/n't on a tensed auxiliary from do-support, and explain how a question fronts the tense-carrying element to C, leaving a gap.

teaching.text: Each auxiliary is the head of its own VP and takes the next VP as its complement, producing a chain of nested VPs.
Only the first verb in the sequence carries the tense feature.
The auxiliary types appear in a fixed order: MOD, then PERF, then PROG, then PASS.

worked_example.sentence: You should have written an essay
worked_example.origin: Original example built to illustrate chained auxiliary VPs.

steps.text: MOD “should” [past] heads the highest VP and is the only tensed verb.
PERF “have” heads the next VP, the complement of the MOD VP.
The lexical VP “written an essay” is the complement of the PERF VP.

source.review_note: Original instructional example source-checked against cited B-R auxiliary VP conventions; not a printed diagram.

guided.prompt: In this worked tree, the PERF VP “have written an essay” is the complement of which node?

options.feedback: Try again. The lexical verb sits lowest. The PERF VP is the complement of the MOD VP.
Yes. Each auxiliary VP takes the next VP as its complement; “should” heads the outer VP.
Try again. The object NP is below the lexical verb, not above the PERF VP.

guided.hint: Look at the highest verb. It is the modal “should”, and the next VP below it is its complement.

opening.prompt: In “You should have written an essay”, which word carries the tense?

options.feedback: “Have” is the perfect auxiliary here. The tense sits on the first verb of the sequence.
Only the first verb of an auxiliary sequence is tensed. “Have” and “written” are not.
“Written” is the lexical verb and carries no tense of its own.

opening.prompt: How many verb phrases (VPs) does “Mina might have finished the report” contain, counting one per auxiliary plus the lexical verb?

options.feedback: Each auxiliary heads its own VP, so there is more than one.
Count every auxiliary VP plus the lexical VP: “might”, “have” and “finished”.
MOD “might”, PERF “have” and lexical “finished” each head a VP.

opening.prompt: In “Byron did not dance”, which word carries both the tense and the negation?

options.feedback: “Do” under the TENSE node carries tense and negation; “dance” is untensed.
The lexical verb is untensed here. The support “do” carries tense and negation.
“Not” supplies the negation, but the tense is on the support word “did”.

opening.prompt: In “Is the cat sleeping?”, what has moved to the front, and what did it leave behind?

options.text: The subject “the cat” moved, leaving a gap before the verb.
options.feedback: The subject stays in place. The tensed auxiliary moves to the front.

options.text: The auxiliary “is” moved to the front, leaving a gap under its PROG node.
options.feedback: The tensed auxiliary fronts to C and its original position becomes a gap.

options.text: The verb “sleeping” moved, leaving no gap.
options.feedback: The lexical verb stays in place. The tensed auxiliary fronts and leaves a gap.

opening.prompt: In “The window was broken by the wind”, what does the by-phrase tell you, and is it required to complete the verb?

options.text: It is a required direct object of “broken”.
options.feedback: The object has become the subject. The by-phrase names the agent and is optional.

options.text: It tells you the tense of the verb.
options.feedback: Tense sits on the auxiliary “was”. The by-phrase names who or what did the action.

options.text: It names the agent and is an optional adjunct, not a required complement.
options.feedback: The verb is passive, and the by-phrase adds the agent as an optional adjunct.

closing.prompt: In “You should have been writing that essay”, list the auxiliary types from top to bottom above the lexical verb.

options.feedback: The modal is highest. Below it come the perfect and then the progressive.
“Should” (MOD), “have” (PERF) and “been” (PROG) each head a VP; only MOD is tensed.
The perfect “have” sits above the progressive “been”.

closing.prompt: Which single verb is tensed in “Nia could have been helping us”?

options.feedback: The tense feature sits only on the first verb of the sequence.
“Have” is a perfect auxiliary with no tense of its own here.
The lexical verb is untensed. Only the first verb carries tense.

closing.prompt: In “Byron would not dance” versus “Byron did not dance”, what structural difference explains where not attaches?

options.text: There is no structural difference; “not” attaches the same way.
options.feedback: Only the first sentence has an auxiliary for “not” to attach to. The second needs do-support.

options.text: The first is passive and the second is active.
options.feedback: Neither sentence is passive. The difference is the presence of a tensed auxiliary.

options.text: The first has a tensed MOD “would” for “not” to attach to; the second has no auxiliary, so do-support supplies an empty “do” under TENSE.
options.feedback: Without an auxiliary, an empty “do” carries tense and negation; the lexical verb stays untensed.

closing.prompt: In “Does Byron dance?”, what moved to C, and where did the gap remain?

options.text: The lexical verb “dance” moved to C, leaving no gap.
options.feedback: The lexical verb stays. “Do” from the TENSE node moves to C.

options.text: “do” moved from the TENSE node to C; the lexical V remains untensed with the gap under the auxiliary position.
options.feedback: Do-support supplies “do”, which fronts to C and leaves a gap where it was.

options.text: The subject “Byron” moved to C, leaving a gap in the subject slot.
options.feedback: The subject stays. The tense-carrier “do” fronts to C and leaves a gap.

closing.prompt: In “Was Kubla extravagant”, why does was behave like an auxiliary even though the main verb be has no other verb to help?

options.text: “Be” always behaves like an auxiliary; the copula fronts to C and leaves a gap under V.
options.feedback: The lexical verb “be” moves to C like an auxiliary, leaving a gap under V.
“Extravagant” is an adjective phrase. “Be” is the verb and behaves like an auxiliary.
No “do” is involved. The verb “be” itself fronts to C.
